title: RCIP job market, October 2026: which occupations are hiring and what they pay
excerpt: Trades and transport, food service, and health and social services make up 52.3% of Job Bank postings in the 14 RCIP communities. Vacancies and wages for the top occupations, and what a posting does and does not tell you about eligibility.
keyTakeaway: Of 1,469 Job Bank postings in the 14 RCIP communities in October 2026, 52.3% were in trades and transport (median at least $27 an hour), food service ($19) or health and social services ($27.63). Harvest labour had the most vacancies (209) but is seasonal, which an RCIP job offer cannot be. A posting is not an eligible offer until the employer, the community's priority list and the wage are checked.
summaryEn: A statistical report on the occupations (NOC 2021) advertised on Job Bank in the 14 Rural Community Immigration Pilot communities in October 2026: top occupations by vacancies with median minimum wages and sample sizes, three steady groups (trades and transport, food service, health and social services), the TEER distribution, and the IRCC tests a posting must still pass.

faq.q: Which occupations are most in demand in RCIP communities?
faq.a: In October 2026, outside seasonal harvest work, the most vacancies were for transport truck drivers (125), food service supervisors (120) and cooks (108), counted from Job Bank postings in the 14 communities.

faq.q: What do trades jobs pay in RCIP communities?
faq.a: Postings in trades and transport stated a median minimum of $27 an hour (323 postings). Heavy-duty equipment mechanics advertised $36.50 and transport truck drivers $30.

faq.q: Can seasonal farm work lead to RCIP?
faq.a: No. IRCC requires an RCIP job offer to be non-seasonal, full time and without an end date. Harvest postings are counted in this report but marked as seasonal.

faq.q: Is a job in a listed occupation automatically eligible for RCIP?
faq.a: No. The employer must be designated by the community, the occupation must be within that community's priorities, and the wage must meet the Job Bank wage for the occupation and region.

content:
Part one of this series showed where jobs were advertised in the 14 Rural Community Immigration Pilot (RCIP) communities in October 2026. This part asks the question that matters more for most people: in which occupations?

Just over half of the 1,469 postings (52.3%) fall into three groups: trades and transport, food service, and health and social services. Trades and transport is the largest and pays a median of at least $27 an hour. Food service is the most widespread and the lowest paid, at $19.

The counts come from Job Bank open data, with 147 copied remote sales ads removed. Occupations are coded with Canada's National Occupational Classification (NOC) 2021.

* Fewer than 20 wages: read the median as an indication only.

Two rows need a warning before anything else.

Harvesting labourers top the list and should be set aside. 16 postings asked for 209 people, one of them for 54, in only 2 communities, both in the BC interior. This is orchard and vineyard work that follows the season. IRCC's rules require an RCIP job offer to be non-seasonal, so these vacancies are outside the program however large the number.

Underground miners are a single hiring round. All 60 vacancies come from 3 postings in 1 community, each for 20 people, at $39 an hour. The demand is real and well paid, but it could be gone next month.

What are the three steady groups?

Set the one-off spikes aside and the same three groups keep appearing across communities.

GroupPostingsVacanciesMedian wage (n)Full timeCommunities (of 14)
Trades and transport325581$27 (323)92.9%14
Food service252396$19 (252)82.5%13
Health and social services191238$27.63 (190)70.2%12

Trades and transport is the largest group and the only one present in all 14 communities, with 92.9% of postings full time. Transport truck drivers lead it (125 vacancies, median $30), followed by heavy-duty equipment mechanics (68 vacancies, $36.50), automotive and truck mechanics, construction labourers, carpenters and welders. Several of these are certified trades in Canada. Certification is a separate step from immigration and differs by province.

Food service is where the sheer number of employers is. Cooks (71 postings in 11 communities) and food service supervisors (68 postings in 10) are advertised almost everywhere, at a median of $19 an hour. Two cautions: these are the lowest wages in the table, and at least two communities' lists show fast food employers as excluded for 2026 (see part one).

Health and social services advertises less than its weight on the designated-employer lists would suggest, and only 70.2% are full time. Licensed practical nurses advertise a median of $36.16, social and community service workers $24.25. Hospitals and health authorities often recruit through their own sites, which Job Bank does not capture.

What happened to retail sales, the original number one?

In the raw data the top occupation was retail salespersons, with 190 postings and a median wage of $53.54 an hour. That figure was produced by the remote sales advertisement described in part one. With it removed, retail salespersons have 60 postings, 99 vacancies and a median of $18.10. That is a normal retail wage, and it puts the occupation fifth.

How does the skill level of a posting connect to RCIP?

Every NOC code belongs to a TEER category from 0 to 5 (training, education, experience and responsibilities). Under IRCC's eligibility rules, the TEER of the job you are offered sets the language level you need and which past work experience counts.

TEER of the jobShare of postingsVacanciesMinimum language level (IRCC)
0 and 18.6% and 9.5%132 and 155CLB 6
2 and 328.9% and 19.2%611 and 506CLB 5
4 and 515.7% and 17%400 and 581CLB 4

Almost half of the postings are in TEER 2 and 3, the band of skilled trades, supervisors and technical roles. For a TEER 5 job, IRCC only accepts experience in the same five-digit NOC code, which makes that route narrower than the low language level suggests. The matching table is in our guide to the RCIP job offer rules.

Does a posting in one of these occupations qualify for RCIP?

Not by itself. Four tests sit between a posting and an eligible job offer, and this data can only speak to the first.

  1. The job's shape. IRCC requires the offer to be full time (at least 30 paid hours a week), non-seasonal and without an end date. 58.4% of postings said both "full time" and "permanent".
  2. The employer. Only a designated employer can make the offer. The open data has no employer names, so we cannot tell you which postings pass.
  3. The community's priorities. Each community sets its own priority sectors and occupations, and recommends only within them. We did not check the postings against the 14 priority lists, and they change. Read your community's current list before relying on any occupation in this report.
  4. The wage. IRCC compares the offered wage with the Job Bank wage for that occupation and region. The medians here are the minimums that postings state. They are not that benchmark.

One more row to treat with care: 30 of the vacancies for livestock workers and farm machinery operators come from a single seasonal posting.

Method and limits

  • One month. These are postings first advertised in October 2026. One month cannot show a trend, and autumn hiring differs from spring hiring.
  • No employer names. Job Bank open data does not say who posted a job. We can count postings in a community, an industry and an occupation; we cannot tell whether a posting came from a designated employer. A posting counted here is not a job offer.
  • Places. A posting is matched to a community by province and town name. 1,067 postings in the national file had no town and could not be placed anywhere.
  • Industry is often missing. 717 of the 1,469 postings (48.8%) came from external job boards without an industry code.
  • Wages are minimums. We take the lowest wage each posting states, per hour. 145 postings give a range whose top is at least one and a half times its bottom, so the real wage may be higher. A median built on fewer than 20 wages is marked as a small sample.
  • Remote sales ads removed. 147 postings were the same work-from-home sales advertisement copied into towns across Canada. They are counted separately and left out of every ranking and median.
  • Listings, not employers. The 2,847 designated-employer listings are rows on the 14 community lists as we read them. Some employers appear more than once; there are 2,830 distinct names. The lists carry different dates.
